help-para-1: OmniUnit is a universal conversion tool with a unit-aware calculator. It supports lots of units — everything you want, and a bunch of stuff you've never heard of. It is SI-focused; all values are stored internally as SI base unit expressions. You can do a simple conversion or paste in a full expression: copy "127.2342 J⋅s⁻¹" from a paper and paste it into the calculator — it will work. Type "7yd" and it parses that too. Units are organized into SI areas to reduce confusion. Power has power-related units: Watts, BTU, etc. No scrolling through thousands of units to find the one you want. Archaic and local units are also supported, but separately. You want tatami to m²? It's got you covered.
help-para-2: It's localized for about a dozen languages and supports the most common number formats worldwide. You don't need to understand English to use it. It defaults to English number formats and the en locale. So you need to get at least that far into the app; otherwise, it's not readable.
help-para-3: The app has four main panes, only two of which are visible at the same time. The default top is the unit conversion. The bottom pane is an RPN unit-aware calculator. You can paste or type in just about anything, and it will work. The conversions for the output of the calculators are limited to SI base and derived units. To convert further, bring the result back to the conversion pane.
help-para-4: There are two additional panes. You can swap out the conversion pane for a build-your-own unit. You can paste in just about anything (like the calculator), and it will reduce that to a base SI expression. You can take it from there. There's also a very simple calculator that will handle most unit arithmetic if you don't like RPN calculators.
help-para-5: The app is a single, standalone .html file. It references no other files and has no links. You can bring it anywhere you have a browser, and it will work. No network or packaging needed. I've also provided a GitHub repository with the project. It's a bog-standard TypeScript/React project. I built it on Replit, but that's not required. You're free to use the .html file or the source code any way you want.
help-github-note: This is the only hyperlink or external reference in the .html distribution. You can click on it or not. It's not part of the app.
help-llm-note: Note: I used an AI assistant to build most of this. It has been tested and includes unit tests. To the best of my knowledge the conversions are correct, but your mileage may vary.
sources-note: Conversion factors and defining relations for every unit, with a reference link for each. Links open in a new tab.
Convert year numbers between calendar er: Convert year numbers between calendar era systems
era-bce-convention: BCE input: choose BCE, or type a negative astronomical year (0 = 1 BCE, −1 = 2 BCE). All conversions go through the astronomical CE year.
note-new-year: New year is not January 1 — value may be off by one (±1)
note-hijri: Tabular Islamic calendar — exact year of 1 Muharram; observation-based calendars may differ by a day or two
note-japanese: Complete nengō list from Taika (645); pre-1873 lunisolar years may be off by one (±1); era-less gaps (654–686, 686–701) are shown under the preceding era
note-japanese-southern: Rival Southern Court era names during the Nanboku-chō period (1336–1392), shown alongside the Northern line in the Japanese Era row
periods-approx-note: All period ranges are approximate ("ca.") and follow conventional scholarly dating.
hijri-date-note: Tabular (arithmetic) Islamic calendar, civil epoch — exact day-level conversion; observation-based calendars may differ by a day or two.
hijri-date-note-astronomical: Tabular (arithmetic) Islamic calendar, astronomical epoch (Thursday, one day earlier than civil) — used by some published tables; observation-based calendars may differ by a day or two.
note-chinese: Orthodox dynastic line only (Han → Qing); rival regimes' era names are omitted; lunisolar years may be off by one (±1)
note-roman-consuls: Eponymous consul pairs, 100 BCE – 14 CE (late Republic through Augustus); ordinary consuls only, suffects omitted
note-saka: New year is not January 1 (±1); Balinese/Javanese Saka shares the same epoch
note-kali-yuga: Epoch 3102 BCE; current-year reckoning; new year is not January 1 (±1)
note-seleucid: Year 1 = 312/311 BCE; Babylonian (spring) reckoning shown — the Macedonian (autumn) count runs one higher (±1)
note-yazdegerdi: From 632 CE; approximate — the 365-day calendar drifts against the solar year
note-mongol: These polities used Chinese era names or the Hijri year rather than a numeric era of their own
era-lookup-out-of-range: Year number is outside this era
rulers-gap-persia: 330–247 BCE: Macedonian & Seleucid rule (Alexander the Great and his successors) — no Persian dynasty on the throne.
rulers-maya-note: The Maya had no single throne: kings ruled concurrently in separate city-states (city noted per ruler).
rulers-curated-note: Curated major rulers only; years between listed reigns show no highlight. "ca." marks approximate reign dates.
rulers-inca-note: Huáscar and Atahualpa reigned concurrently during the 1529–1532 civil war; the Vilcabamba rump state (1533–1572) survived the Spanish conquest as a coda.
